frameworks.name: Core Four Customer Acquisition Methods
frameworks.definition: Four sequenced channels for getting customers: (1) warm outreach one-to-one, (2) free content posting, (3) cold outreach one-to-one, (4) paid ads one-to-many.

frameworks.name: Hook-Retain-Reward Content Framework
frameworks.definition: Three-part content structure: hook (first 3 seconds to stop the scroll), retain (list, steps, or story to hold attention), reward (funny moment, call-to-action, or shareable payoff at the end).

frameworks.name: Four Returns From Free Work
frameworks.definition: Every free service recipient can generate value in four ways: (1) they become a paying customer, (2) they leave a review, (3) they refer a friend, (4) they give feedback that improves the offering.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that for anyone starting a service business with no reputation or track record, giving the service away for free to the first 5-10 people is the correct framing because your time has zero market value until you have a proven track record; framing free work as the customer doing you a favor (not as you being generous) prevents the resentment that destroys early client relationships.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: service business
zero track record
no existing customers or reviews
claims.mechanism: Without a reputation, the seller's time has no established market value; free work buys practice, feedback, and social proof simultaneously, which are the three inputs needed to build a track record; resentment arises only when the seller wrongly believes the free work is a sacrifice rather than an investment.
bounded_by: Does not apply once the founder has a proven track record and paying customers

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that one free customer in a neighborhood unlocks every other door in that neighborhood because name-dropping a mutual neighbor (e.g., 'I work with the Johnsons') dramatically increases the probability that a stranger will open the door, extend the conversation, and convert, because they treat you as someone their neighbor vouches for rather than a cold stranger.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: door-to-door or neighborhood cold outreach
one free or paid anchor customer already in the geography
claims.mechanism: Social proof from a shared connection collapses stranger distrust; people are reliably more polite and more attentive when they believe the person has already been approved by someone in their social graph.
bounded_by: Requires at least one real anchor customer in the relevant geography or social group

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that in warm outreach (calling people you know), asking 'do you know anybody who needs X?' rather than 'do you want X?' dramatically improves conversion because the indirect frame removes the social pressure of a direct solicitation, making the person more likely to engage and refer.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: warm outreach to existing contacts
early-stage no-reputation selling
claims.mechanism: Asking if they know someone rather than asking if they personally want the service removes the target's need to defend against a sales pitch; they become a helper rather than a prospect, which reduces psychological resistance.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that requesting a three-way text introduction on the spot (rather than asking someone to 'pass your name along later') doubles lead capture rate from warm outreach because it eliminates the forgetting friction that kills most referral promises, and also causes the newly-introduced stranger to be significantly more polite since a mutual contact is visibly present in the thread.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: warm outreach
requesting a referral in real time during the conversation
claims.mechanism: A promise to introduce later requires the referrer to remember, initiate, and context-switch; a live three-way text happens in the moment with zero friction; the visible presence of the mutual contact acts as a social chaperone that reduces the referred stranger's rudeness.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that no-based questions (e.g., 'Would you be opposed to...?' or 'Would it be a huge inconvenience if...?') produce a slightly higher yes rate across large populations than direct yes-based questions (e.g., 'Do you want...?'), because people have a lower threshold for saying no than yes.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any sales context where a direct solicitation is being made
claims.mechanism: People are cognitively biased toward declining requests; reframing the desired answer as a denial (saying 'no' to mean 'yes I agree') lowers the friction of commitment.
bounded_by: Alex Hormozi notes that yes-based questions also work and he has closed many sales using them; the effect is marginal across large populations, not binary

claims.text: Alex Hormozi states that after a prospect says yes, every additional word spoken by the seller increases the probability that the prospect reverses their decision; the correct behavior is to immediately move to the next action step (e.g., going to the truck, writing down card information) and say nothing else that could reopen deliberation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any sales close where verbal confirmation has been obtained

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that when a prospect already has a competitor providing the service you are selling, they are actually more likely to convert than a prospect with no provider, because their willingness to pay for the category is proven.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: door-to-door or cold outreach where prospect has an existing provider
claims.mechanism: An existing provider proves category demand; the seller's task shifts from creating demand to offering a superior deal, not from educating a skeptic.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that warm outreach (calling people you know) has two hard ceilings that cap growth: (1) the finite number of hours in a day you can make calls, and (2) the finite size of your total network (email list + phone contacts + social followers across all platforms), which for most early-stage founders sums to roughly 1,000 people reachable within 10 days at 100 contacts per day.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: early-stage founder using warm outreach as primary acquisition channel

numbers.axis: total warm network size for early-stage founder

anchors.value: ~1,000 contacts across email list, phone contacts, and all social platforms

bounded_by: Re-reaching the same contacts later is possible but yields diminishing returns after first pass

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that the first three seconds of a content video are the most important three seconds because approximately 80% of viewers decide whether to keep watching within that window; all creative and testing effort should be concentrated on the hook.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: short-form or mid-form video content on social platforms
claims.mechanism: Viewer intent is resolved in the first few seconds of a video; if the hook fails to establish relevance or curiosity, the platform algorithm and the viewer both route attention elsewhere.

numbers.axis: viewer drop-off decision timing in a paid ad or content video

anchors.value: remaining 20% are substantially more likely to watch through

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that in free content and paid ads, using three named benefits or pain points creates a mental scaffolding that keeps viewers watching because it opens a loop ('you said three things, I need to hear all three') that is more effective than an unstructured continuous narrative.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: any video content or paid ad with a retention goal
claims.mechanism: The human need for closure on an explicitly stated list forces continued attention; announcing 'three things' commits the viewer to watch until they have heard all three to resolve the cognitive open loop.

numbers.axis: number of named items that optimally opens a retention loop

anchors.region: tested by speaker across fitness, nutrition, accountability programs

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that people need to be reminded of ideas far more than they need to be taught new ones; repeating core content themes across formats (tweet, reel, video, podcast, caption) is not laziness but reflects the reality that no audience member consumes 100% of a creator's output 100% of the time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: content creators with a recurring publishing cadence

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that for paid advertising, the visual identity of the person in the ad (gender, age, setting, dress) functions as a filtering mechanism that attracts or repels specific audience segments before any word is spoken, and that running ads featuring multiple different representative people can double or triple lead flow without changing any other variable.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: paid social advertising where the seller targets a specific avatar
claims.mechanism: Viewers pattern-match the person in the ad against their own identity; if the person looks like them or like the kind of person they trust, they self-select in; if not, they scroll past. The visual callout does avatar filtering before any spoken hook.

numbers.axis: lift in lead flow from diversifying ad talent

anchors.region: two to four different people in ads

bounded_by: Effect is specific to social paid ads where visual identity is displayed immediately; may not generalize to text-based or voice-only channels

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that in a paid ad, the guarantee should be placed adjacent to the pain point it most directly addresses rather than at a fixed position (always first or always last), because the guarantee has maximum persuasive force when the viewer's pain is most actively aroused.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: paid advertising for a service business
ad contains multiple pain points and a guarantee
claims.mechanism: A guarantee resolves the specific fear it names; placing it immediately after raising that fear maximizes the emotional contrast between 'this pain exists' and 'this fear is now removed.'

claims.text: Alex Hormozi claims that in cold outreach (knocking doors, cold DMs, cold calls), the seller's biggest lever for increasing yes rate is the quality and generosity of the initial offer (big, fast value), not script quality, because strangers have no trust baseline and require a strong enough incentive to act despite zero prior relationship.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: cold outreach to strangers with no prior relationship
claims.mechanism: Without trust, prospects require an asymmetrically favorable offer to overcome the default skepticism toward unknown vendors; a superior offer compensates for absence of social proof.
bounded_by: In warm outreach where trust exists, offer quality is less critical; in paid ads, creative quality matters at least as much as offer quality

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that insufficient reply volume in cold outreach is always solved by increasing outreach volume rather than improving message quality, because the constraint is the sheer number of nos the seller is willing to absorb, and automation and collaboration are the two levers to increase volume without proportional founder time.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: cold outreach campaign where reply rate is acceptable but absolute reply count is too low
bounded_by: If reply rate itself is near zero (not just reply count), volume alone will not fix it; script or offer quality must be addressed first

claims.text: Alex Hormozi argues that content-engaged leads (people who liked, commented on, or shared a piece of content) are higher-quality warm leads than unsolicited cold contacts, because public engagement demonstrates genuine interest and gives the seller a non-invasive reason to initiate contact.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: content-based lead generation where engagement is tracked
claims.mechanism: Engagement is a behavioral signal of interest; reaching out to someone who engaged is socially justified by the engagement itself, lowering the psychological barrier for the prospect and the seller.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi recommends that early-stage content creators reframe their view count in terms of physical room size (e.g., 17 views equals a full classroom), because the comparison to viral clips creates demotivating distortion, while the room metaphor makes the equivalent real-world event feel clearly worthwhile.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: early-stage content creator with small audience
view counts below several hundred

numbers.axis: video view count mapped to real-world audience equivalent

anchors.value: comparison that is demotivating at early stage

claims.text: Alex Hormozi asserts that building your own contact list by scraping sources manually (Yelp, Google Maps, Facebook groups, Reddit forums) produces higher response rates than purchased software lists or broker lists, because self-assembled lists are untouched by competing outreach campaigns that have fatigued the same contacts.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: cold outreach to businesses or consumers
comparing list assembly methods
claims.mechanism: Software-vendor and broker lists are sold to multiple buyers; by the time a seller uses them, contacts have been hit repeatedly by competitors, generating fatigue and lower open and response rates; a self-scraped list is exclusive to the scraper until others find the same sources.
bounded_by: Self-assembly is more time-intensive; for very large volume campaigns, software or broker lists may still be net-positive even at lower response rates

examples.text: Alex Hormozi demonstrates warm outreach by calling a contact named Caleb who is at a wedding. He uses a personalized opener (acknowledging the wedding), pivots to asking whether anyone is taking out Caleb's trash, frames the initial offer as five to ten free trials in exchange for a review if the service is good or honest feedback if it is not, and then immediately asks Caleb for a three-way text introduction to other people at the wedding who might also not have trash service. Caleb agrees to both the free service and the intro. This demonstrates the full warm-outreach script: personalized opener, indirect ask for referrals, free-trial offer framed as the prospect doing the seller a favor, and real-time three-way intro request.

Alex Hormozi demonstrates door-to-door cold outreach across three neighbor scenarios. In the first, he tells the homeowner he works with the Johnsons (the neighbor) and asks whether they have someone taking their trash out. The homeowner says no, he asks a no-based question ('Would you be opposed to...?'), gets a yes, and moves immediately to collecting trash without further selling. In the second scenario, the homeowner already has a provider; Hormozi pivots by asking whether that provider is as friendly and whether they offer a free first month, then offers both, converting the prospect at $29/month after the free period. In the third scenario, the homeowner does not answer or says no, and Hormozi narrates that getting a no costs nothing and the next door is the next attempt. Together these three scenarios illustrate the branching decision tree for door-to-door cold outreach: anchor in a mutual neighbor, no-based close, handle the existing-provider objection, and accept nos without loss.

Alex Hormozi produces two short-form content videos for the trash business. The first is titled 'Want to know the best way to get your husband to take the trash out?' and teaches no-based questioning and positive reinforcement, ending with a soft call to action for 1-800-ALEX-TRASH. The second opens with 'Trash is gross to everyone but me,' uses three numbered tips (bag method, tools, calling Hormozi), and ends with a joke close. In the breakdown, he identifies each video's hook (the first three seconds), retention mechanism (list or numbered steps that open cognitive loops), and reward (shareable humor or call-to-action). He notes the second hook works because it is weird and curiosity-provoking. These two examples illustrate the hook-retain-reward framework applied to a single niche across two different hook styles.

Alex Hormozi produces a paid ad for the trash business that opens with three visual hook variations ('Are you backed up in trash?', 'You smell that smell?', 'Is this you every trash day?'), agitates multiple pain points (missing pickup day, trash smell, low-skilled rude workers, missing children's activities because of chores), then presents three differentiators: never miss a pickup with a three-free-months guarantee if they do, always on time, and always polite ('Yes sir, no sir, yes ma'am, no ma'am'). The CTA is 'Click the link or call 1-800-ALEX-TRASH.' Hormozi explains each structural decision: why the guarantee is placed next to the biggest pain point rather than at the end, how multiple yes-based hooks can funnel into the same body of the ad, and why visual call-outs (man with gloves, trash in background) do avatar filtering before any spoken word.

practices.text: When doing warm outreach, open with a genuine personalized observation about what the contact is currently doing (e.g., noticing they are at a wedding) before pivoting to your business topic; this creates rapport before the ask.

When starting content for a local service business, target one of two content angles: (1) consumer tips that make the prospect's life better independent of hiring you, or (2) content targeting potential hires to attract talent. Both build authority; they can be interspersed.

For paid ads targeting a specific avatar, use visual cues (dress, setting, person demographics in the video) that match the target customer so that the visual callout filters the right viewers before any spoken word.

When building a cold outreach list, prioritize self-assembled lists scraped from Yelp, Google Maps, Facebook groups, and Reddit forums over purchased software or broker lists, as self-assembled lists are not fatigued by competitor outreach.

In any sales conversation, as soon as the prospect says yes, stop talking and move immediately to the next action step (collecting payment, writing down card details, beginning the service); everything said after the yes increases reversal risk.

Frame free trial work as the prospect doing the seller a favor rather than the seller being generous; this prevents the resentment that emerges when founders believe they are owed gratitude for giving away work they have no established market rate for.
